p.src: When Baoyu came out into the courtyard, several pages who served Jia Zheng rushed up and seized him around the waist. “It was thanks to us that the Master was pleased with you today,” they all said. “The Old Lady sent people out several times to ask how things were going, and each time we told her that he was pleased. Otherwise, if she had called you inside, you would never have had the chance to display your talent. Everyone says the poems you composed just now are finer than anyone else’s. You have won such high praise today. You ought to reward us.” Baoyu laughed. “A string of cash for each of you.” “Who cares about a mere string of cash?” they cried. Give us that purse instead.” As they spoke, one came forward to untie his purse and another his fan case; without allowing him any say, they stripped away everything he wore at his waist. Then they said, “Now let us escort him back properly.” One of them lifted him into his arms, while the others crowded around and carried him as far as the inner gate of Grandmother Jia’s quarters. By then Grandmother Jia had already sent people several times to see how he was faring. His nurses and maids came hurrying after him. Once they had seen Grandmother Jia and learned that he had not been given a hard time, they were naturally delighted.

p.src: A little later, Xiren brought him some tea. Seeing that not one of the things he had worn remained, she laughed and said, “That shameless lot must have taken all your things off you again.” Hearing this, Lin Daiyu came over to look and saw that it was indeed all gone. She asked Baoyu, “Did you give them the purse I made for you too? If you ever want anything from me again, you will not get it!” With that, she returned to her room in a huff, took up the fragrant sachet Baoyu had asked her to make a few days before—which was only half finished—and angrily began cutting it apart. Seeing her anger, Baoyu realized that something was wrong and hurried after her, but she had already cut it. Baoyu had already seen this sachet. Though unfinished, it was exquisitely made and had cost her a great deal of labor. Now that she had cut it up for no good reason, he too could not help feeling vexed. He hurriedly opened his collar, untied from the front of his red inner jacket the purse Daiyu had given him, and held it out for her to see. “Look! What is this? When have I ever given away anything you made for me?” When Lin Daiyu saw how carefully he treasured it, wearing it inside his clothes evidently to prevent anyone from taking it, she regretted her rashness in cutting up the sachet before she knew the truth. Ashamed as well as angry, she lowered her head and said nothing. Baoyu said, “There was no need for you to cut it up. I know you simply cannot be bothered to make me anything. Why do I not return this purse to you as well?” As he spoke, he tossed it into her lap and turned to leave. This made Daiyu angrier still. Her voice choked and her breath caught; tears welled up and rolled down her cheeks as she picked up the purse and tried to cut it too. Seeing this, Baoyu quickly turned back and snatched it from her. “Dear sister,” he said with a smile, “please spare it!” Daiyu flung down the scissors and said as she wiped away her tears, “Do not be affectionate one moment and cruel the next. If you are angry with me, just let me go. What sort of behavior is this?” Still angry, she climbed onto the bed, lay down facing the wall, and wiped away her tears. But Baoyu came up to apologize, calling her “dear sister” over and over, until she could resist him no longer.

The nurses and maids hurriedly replied, “He is in Miss Lin’s room.” “Good, good, good!” said Grandmother Jia on hearing this. Let the brother and sister amuse themselves together. p.src: At this time, Lady Wang's quarters were bustling with activity. It turned out that Jia Qiang had returned from Suzhou after purchasing twelve young girls, hiring instructors, and procuring costumes and all the other necessities. By then, Aunt Xue had moved to a secluded residence in the northeast, leaving Pear Fragrance Court vacant; it had already been renovated, and the instructors were ordered to train the girls there in opera. Several women of the household who had once trained as singers and performers—though all were now white-haired old dames—were also assigned to supervise and manage them. Jia Qiang was placed in overall charge of their daily receipts and expenditures, as well as the accounts for every large and small item they required. Then the wife of Lin Zhixiao came to report: “We have sought out and engaged ten young Buddhist nuns, and the young Daoist nuns have also been secured. Even the twenty newly made Daoist robes are ready. There is also a young woman who practices the religious life without shaving her head. She is a native of Suzhou, and her ancestors belonged to a family of scholars and officials. This girl was sickly from childhood, and although her family purchased many substitutes to enter religion in her stead, none proved effective. Only when she herself entered the religious life did she finally recover. She therefore practices without shaving her head; she is just eighteen this year, and her religious name is Miaoyu. Both her parents are now dead, and she is attended only by two elderly nurses and one young maid. She is highly accomplished in letters, already knows the scriptures without further instruction, and is exceptionally beautiful as well. Having heard that the capital, Chang'an, possessed relics of Guanyin and ancient scriptures written on pattra leaves, she came north with her teacher last year and is now living at Muni Convent outside the western gate. Her teacher was highly skilled in interpreting the divine numerology of the Earlier Heaven, but passed into nirvana last winter. Miaoyu originally intended to escort her teacher's coffin back home, but as her teacher lay dying, she left these final words: ‘It would not be fitting for you to return home to live. Remain here in quiet seclusion, and in time your destiny will naturally unfold.’ And so she did not return home after all.” Before the report was finished, Lady Wang said, “If that is so, why do we not invite her here?” The wife of Lin Zhixiao replied, “We did invite her, but she said, ‘In the mansions of marquises and dukes, people are sure to use their rank and power to coerce others. I will never go.’” Lady Wang laughed. “Since she is the daughter of an official family, it is only natural that she should be somewhat proud. Why not send her a formal invitation?” The wife of Lin Zhixiao assented and withdrew, then ordered the correspondence secretary to write an invitation for Miaoyu. The next day, people were sent with a carriage and sedan chair to fetch her, but that belongs to what follows and must for now be set aside.

p.src: Lady Wang and the others remained in a daily whirl of activity until nearly the end of the tenth month, when fortunately everything was finally ready: the supervisors of every department had settled their accounts; all the antiques and curios had been arranged; and those charged with procuring birds and animals had purchased everything from cranes and peacocks to deer, rabbits, chickens, geese, and the like, which were distributed throughout the garden and raised wherever they best suited the scenery. Jia Qiang's troupe had also rehearsed twenty assorted operatic pieces, while the young Buddhist and Daoist nuns had all learned to recite several volumes of scriptures and incantations. Only then did Jia Zheng feel somewhat relieved. He invited Grandmother Jia and the others into the garden once more, and after every detail had been considered and the decorations properly adjusted, there was no longer the least omission or impropriety. Jia Zheng then chose an auspicious day to submit a memorial to the throne. On the day the memorial was submitted, an imperial rescript in vermilion granted the petition: on the fifteenth day of the first month of the following year, the Lantern Festival, Consort Jia was graciously permitted to visit her family. After the Jia household received this gracious decree, everyone became busier than ever, working day and night, and they did not even celebrate the New Year properly.

p.src: In the blink of an eye, the Lantern Festival drew near. Beginning on the eighth day of the first month, eunuchs came ahead to inspect the arrangements: where the Consort would change clothes, where she would sit at ease, where she would receive formal homage, where the banquet would be held, and where she would retire to rest. Eunuchs charged with inspecting the premises, overseeing security, and other duties also arrived with many junior eunuchs. They secured each location, erected screens and curtains, and instructed the Jia household where its members were to withdraw, where they were to kneel, where meals were to be presented, and where reports were to be made, together with a host of other ceremonial regulations. Outside, officials from the Ministry of Works and the military commissioners of the Five Metropolitan Wards swept the streets and drove away idlers. Jia She and the others supervised the craftsmen in making ornamental lanterns, fireworks, and the like, and by the fourteenth everything was securely in place. That night, not a soul in the household, from highest to lowest, slept at all.

p.src: At the fifth watch on the fifteenth, Grandmother Jia and all the others who held rank dressed in full ceremonial attire appropriate to their stations. Everywhere in the garden, coiling dragons seemed to dance upon the canopies and colored phoenixes to fly across the curtains; gold and silver flashed in splendor, jewels vied in brilliance, tripods burned the fragrance of lilies, and vases held blossoms of everlasting spring. All was so still that not a cough could be heard. Jia She and the others waited outside the west street gate, while Grandmother Jia and the rest waited outside the main gate of the Rong Mansion. The streets and alley entrances were all tightly screened off with curtains. Just as they were growing impatient with waiting, a eunuch suddenly arrived on a tall horse. Grandmother Jia hurriedly had him brought in and asked for news. The eunuch said, “It is much too early yet! At the first quarter of the hour of the Goat, Her Highness will finish her evening meal; at the second quarter of mid-Goat hour, she must go to Baoling Palace to worship the Buddha; and at the first quarter of the hour of the Rooster, she will enter Daming Palace to attend the banquet and view the lanterns before requesting permission to depart. I fear she will not set out until the beginning of the hour of the Dog.” On hearing this, Xifeng said, “In that case, Old Ancestress and Madam, please return to your rooms for now. It will not be too late to come back when the time draws near.” Grandmother Jia and the others therefore went to rest for the time being, leaving Xifeng entirely responsible for managing the garden. They also ordered the attendants on duty to take the eunuchs away and serve them food and wine.

p.src: Presently, servants were ordered to carry in candles by the shoulder-load and light the lamps everywhere. No sooner had they finished than the sound of galloping horses was heard outside. Before long, a dozen or so eunuchs came running up, panting and clapping their hands. The other eunuchs understood the signal and knew that Her Highness had arrived; each took up his appointed position. Jia She led the sons and nephews of the clan to wait outside the west street gate, while Grandmother Jia led all the women of the clan to receive the visitor outside the main gate. For a long while, all remained perfectly still and silent. Suddenly, a pair of red-robed eunuchs appeared, riding slowly toward them. They dismounted at the west street gate, had their horses led beyond the enclosing screens, and then stood with lowered hands, facing west. After another long interval, a second pair arrived and did likewise. Soon a dozen or so pairs had arrived, and only then could the faint strains of delicate music be heard. There followed, pair after pair, dragon banners and phoenix fans, ornaments of pheasant feathers and kui-dragon heads, and gilded hand-braziers burning imperial incense. Then came a curved-handled golden parasol adorned with seven phoenixes, beneath which could be seen the ceremonial headdress, robe, girdle, and shoes. Other eunuchs on duty carried fragrant beads, embroidered kerchiefs, rinsing basins, fly-whisks, and similar articles. When all these companies had passed, eight eunuchs at last came slowly forward, bearing a golden-yellow palanquin with a golden roof and embroidered phoenixes. Grandmother Jia and the others hastily knelt by the roadside. Several eunuchs had already dashed forward to help Grandmother Jia, Lady Xing, and Lady Wang to their feet. The palanquin was borne through the main gate and then eastward through the ceremonial gate. When it reached the entrance to a courtyard, a fly-whisk-bearing eunuch knelt and requested that Her Highness alight and change her clothes. The palanquin was therefore carried inside. The eunuchs withdrew, leaving only the court ladies and imperial attendants to escort Yuanchun from it. The courtyard was ablaze with lanterns of every color, all exquisitely fashioned from gauze and silk. Above hung a tablet-shaped lantern bearing the four characters “Embody Benevolence and Bathe in Virtue.” Yuanchun entered the room, changed her clothes, and, emerging again, mounted the palanquin to proceed into the garden. Throughout the garden, fragrant smoke curled through a riot of blossoms and colors; everywhere lanterns shone upon one another, while strains of delicate music continually swelled. No words could exhaust the spectacle of peace and prosperity, wealth and elegance. At this point, the Stone recalled its former desolation and loneliness beneath Greensickness Peak in the Great Waste Mountain. Had the scabby-headed monk and the lame Taoist not brought it here, how could it ever have witnessed such magnificence? I had intended to compose a “Rhapsody on Lanterns and Moonlight” and a “Hymn to the Imperial Homecoming” to commemorate the events of this day, but feared falling into the hackneyed conventions of other books. Indeed, even a rhapsody and a hymn could not fully convey the wonders of this scene; and without them, discerning readers can surely imagine its sumptuous splendor for themselves. It is therefore better to spare the labor and ink and return to our proper story.

p.src: Now, as Consort Jia viewed from her palanquin all the splendor within and without the garden, she silently sighed at such lavish extravagance. Presently, she saw a fly-whisk-bearing eunuch kneel and invite her to board a boat, whereupon she descended from the palanquin. A clear stream wound away like a swimming dragon. The stone balustrades on either bank were hung with colored crystal and glass lanterns, whose light resembled silver blossoms and snowy waves. Though the willows, apricots, and other trees above bore neither leaves nor flowers, both had been fashioned to match their natural forms from pith, satin, paper, and silk and fixed to the branches; several lanterns also hung from every tree. Even the lotuses, water plants, wild ducks, egrets, and other things upon the pond had been fashioned from shells, feathers, and similar materials. The lanterns above and below vied in brilliance: it was truly a world of crystal, a universe of jewels. p.src: Before Consort Jia entered the palace, she too had been brought up from childhood by Grandmother Jia. Later, when Baoyu was born, she was the eldest sister and he the youngest brother. Mindful that their mother had borne this son only as she approached old age, Consort Jia cherished Baoyu and treated him differently from all her other brothers. Both lived with their grandmother and were never apart for even a moment. Before Baoyu entered school, when he was only three or four, Consort Jia had already guided him by the hand and instructed him by word of mouth, teaching him several books and filling his mind with thousands of written characters. Though sister and brother by formal relationship, in affection they were like mother and son. After entering the palace, she repeatedly sent messages to their parents: “You must take the greatest care in raising him. Without strictness he will never amount to anything, but excessive severity may cause some mishap and bring anxiety upon his parents.” Her tender concern and devoted love for him never left her for an instant. A few days earlier, Jia Zheng had heard Baoyu's tutor privately praise the boy's abundance of unconventional talent. Jia Zheng did not believe him, but as the garden had just happened to be completed, he ordered Baoyu to devise its inscriptions, partly to test whether his thoughts and sensibilities were refined or vulgar. Though the tablets and couplets he devised were no masterpieces, they had some merit as the work of a young child. It would of course have been no great difficulty to commission a celebrated writer instead, yet on reflection, that would have lacked the charm of something produced within the family itself. Moreover, when Consort Jia saw them and learned they were the work of her beloved brother, they might fulfill the earnest hopes she had always placed in him. For these reasons, Baoyu's tablets and couplets were adopted after all. Although he had not finished composing them all that day, he had subsequently supplied the missing ones.

p.src: After tea had been presented three times, Consort Jia descended from her seat and the music ceased. She withdrew to a side hall to change her clothes, after which her carriage was prepared to leave the garden for the family visit. On reaching Grandmother Jia’s principal apartments, she wished to perform the courtesies due within a family, but Grandmother Jia and the others hastily knelt and repeatedly begged her to desist. Her eyes brimming with tears, Consort Jia at last came forward to greet them. With one hand she supported Grandmother Jia and with the other Lady Wang. All three had hearts full of things to say, yet none could utter a word; they could only sob and weep together. Lady Xing, Li Wan, Wang Xifeng, and the three sisters Yingchun, Tanchun, and Xichun stood gathered around them, shedding silent tears. Only after a long while did Consort Jia master her grief and force a smile. Consoling Grandmother Jia and Lady Wang, she said, “Since you sent me that day to a place where I could see none of you, it has been no easy matter for me to come home today and spend a little time with my mother and the family. Instead of talking and laughing together, why have we all begun to cry? Once I leave again, who knows how long it will be before I can return!” At these words, she could not keep herself from choking with sobs once more. Lady Xing and the others hurried forward to comfort them. Grandmother Jia and the others invited Consort Jia to take her seat; each then came forward in turn to greet her, which inevitably brought on another bout of weeping. Afterward, the male stewards and officials of the eastern and western mansions paid their respects outside the hall, followed by the wives of the two households’ stewards and their attendant maids. Consort Jia then asked, “Why do I not see Aunt Xue, Baochai, or Daiyu?” Lady Wang replied, “As relations from outside the household who hold no rank, they did not dare enter without permission.” On hearing this, Consort Jia promptly ordered that they be invited in at once. Presently Aunt Xue and the others entered. They were about to perform the formal court obeisance, but Consort Jia waived it and had them come forward to exchange greetings after their long separation. Baoqin and the other maids whom Consort Jia had originally taken into the palace also came forward and kowtowed. Grandmother Jia and the others hastily helped them rise and ordered that they be entertained in another room. The eunuchs in charge, the imperial attendants, the ladies-in-waiting, and their respective retinues were entertained separately at the Ningguo mansion and at Jia She’s residence; only three or four young eunuchs remained to attend Consort Jia. Mother, daughter, and sisters spoke at length of their separation and of private family affairs. Jia Zheng then came to the far side of the curtain to inquire after her well-being, and Consort Jia had the curtain lowered while the prescribed salutations were exchanged. Then, through the curtain, she said tearfully to her father, “A farming family, though living only on salted vegetables and clothed in homespun, can still enjoy the happiness of being together as kin. We, though raised to the very pinnacle of wealth and honor, are scattered from our own flesh and blood, and there is ultimately no joy in it!” Jia Zheng also replied through his tears, “I, your servant, come from an obscure and humble house, a flock of common doves and crows; how could I ever have dreamed that among us would appear the auspicious phoenix? Now Your Highness has received Heaven’s favor from above and displayed the virtue of our ancestors below. All this is because the rare essence of mountains, rivers, sun, and moon, and the accumulated virtue of distant generations of our forebears, have converged in one person, bringing good fortune even to my wife and me. Moreover, His Majesty manifests Heaven and Earth’s great virtue of bringing forth all living things and bestows a boundless grace unknown in any age. Even if I were to spill my brains upon the ground, how could a subject repay even one ten-thousandth of it? Beyond remaining diligent and vigilant from dawn till dusk and serving faithfully in my office, I can only pray that our sovereign may live for ten thousand years; this would be the common blessing of all the people under Heaven.

p.src: At that point Baoyu had still not finished. He had completed only the two poems on “The Xiaoxiang Lodge” and “The Hengwu Court” and was composing the one on “Happy Red Court”; in his draft appeared the line, “Green jade remains curled in spring.” Baochai happened to glance over and see it. While no one else was paying attention, she quickly turned back, gave him a gentle push, and whispered, “Her Highness disliked the four characters ‘red fragrance and green jade’ and changed them to ‘joyous red and refreshing green.’ If you insist on using ‘green jade’ now, will it not look as though you are deliberately challenging her? Besides, there are many expressions for banana leaves. Think of another character and change it.” Hearing this, Baoyu wiped away his sweat and said, “At the moment I cannot recall any suitable allusion or source at all.” Baochai smiled. “Simply change the character ‘jade’ in ‘green jade’ to ‘wax.’” “Is there a source for ‘green wax’?” asked Baoyu. At this question, Baochai quietly clicked her tongue, nodded, and smiled. “So tonight this is the best you can do! When the day comes for you to answer questions in the Golden Hall, I daresay you will even have forgotten ‘Zhao, Qian, Sun, Li’! The first line of Tang poet Qian Xu's poem on the banana plant reads, ‘A cold smokeless candle, the green wax dry.’ Can you really have forgotten it?” On hearing this, Baoyu suddenly saw everything clearly and laughed. “I deserve to die! I deserve to die! I could not recall something ready to hand and right before my eyes. You truly deserve to be called my ‘teacher of a single character.’ From now on I shall call you Master and never Elder Sister again.” Baochai also laughed softly. “Hurry up and put it into your poem instead of prattling on about elder and younger sisters. Who is your elder sister? Your elder sister is the lady up there in the yellow robe, yet here you are claiming me as one again.” Even as she joked with him, she feared that their banter might delay his work, so she withdrew and walked away. Baoyu had no choice but to carry on, and so completed three poems in all.

p.src: Jia Qiang hurried to arrange the performances. Each voice seemed capable of splitting stone, and every dance possessed the grace of a celestial enchantress. Though all was feigned in costume and gesture, they portrayed every shade of sorrow and joy. They had only just finished when a eunuch entered carrying a golden tray of cakes and other delicacies and asked, “Which one is Lingguan?” Jia Qiang knew at once that these were gifts for Lingguan. Delighted, he hurried to receive them and ordered her to kowtow. The eunuch continued, “Her Highness has decreed: ‘Lingguan was excellent. Let her perform two more scenes, whichever two she pleases.’” Jia Qiang readily assented and told Lingguan to perform “A Walk in the Garden” and “The Startled Dream.” Lingguan maintained that these two scenes did not belong to her proper role and stubbornly refused, insisting instead on performing “The Tryst” and “The Lovers’ Quarrel.” Unable to bend her will, Jia Qiang had no choice but to let her do as she wished. Consort Jia was greatly pleased and ordered that “the girl must not be treated harshly, but carefully trained.” She awarded her an additional two lengths of palace satin, two purses, pieces of gold and silver, and assorted foods. The banquet was then cleared away, and she resumed her tour of the places she had not yet visited. Suddenly seeing a Buddhist temple encircled by hills, she hastened to wash her hands afresh, went in to burn incense and worship the Buddha, and inscribed a plaque: “Merciful Vessel Across the Sea of Suffering.” She also granted special favors to the secluded Buddhist nuns and Taoist priestesses.

p.src: Presently a eunuch knelt and reported, “All the gifts are prepared. Your Highness is requested to inspect the list according to custom.” He then presented an abbreviated inventory. Consort Jia examined it from beginning to end, found everything in good order, and commanded that it be carried out accordingly. The eunuch withdrew and distributed each item in turn. Lady Jia’s gifts were one gold and one jade sceptre of good fortune, an eaglewood walking stick, a string of aloeswood prayer beads, four lengths of palace satin patterned “Wealth and Everlasting Spring,” four lengths of palace silk patterned “Long Life and Unending Blessings,” ten purple-gold ingots bearing the rebus “May All Be Settled as You Wish,” and ten silver ingots bearing the rebus “May Abundance and Celebration Be Yours.” The portions for Lady Xing and Lady Wang were the same except for the four kinds of gifts comprising the sceptres, walking sticks, and beads. Jia Jing, Jia She, Jia Zheng, and the others each received two newly published imperial books, two boxes of fine ink, two gold and two silver wine cups, and the same formal gifts as above. Baochai, Daiyu, and the other young ladies each received one new book, one fine inkstone, and two pairs of newly fashioned gold and silver ingots. Baoyu received the same. Jia Lan received two gold and silver neck rings and two pairs of gold and silver ingots. You-shi, Li Wan, Xifeng, and the others each received four gold and silver ingots and four lengths of formal gift cloth. A further twenty-four lengths of formal gift cloth and one hundred strings of standard cash were bestowed upon the wet nurses and maids in the apartments of Lady Jia, Lady Wang, and the young ladies. Jia Zhen, Jia Lian, Jia Huan, Jia Rong, and the others each received one formal gift and a pair of gold ingots. The remaining hundred lengths of colored satin, one thousand taels of gold and silver, imperial wine, and sumptuous banquet fare were bestowed on all those of the eastern and western mansions who had supervised construction, arranged the furnishings, attended to service in the garden, managed the plays, or tended the lamps. An additional five hundred strings of standard cash were bestowed upon the cooks, actors, acrobats, and workers of the various trades.
